title: Κλῆρος
titleEn: The Lots in the Helmet — Iliad 7.92–180
about: Nobody answers Hector’s challenge until Menelaus, shamed by the silence, rises and says he will fight him, leaving the result to the gods. Agamemnon takes him by the hand and talks him out of it: Hector is the better man, and even Achilles shrinks from meeting him. Menelaus gives way, and Nestor rises to reproach the Achaeans. He says old Peleus would groan to see them cower, tells how as a young man he killed the giant Ereuthalion, who wore the armour of Areithous the club-wielder, and wishes he were that young again. Nine men stand up: Agamemnon, Diomedes, the two Ajaxes, Idomeneus, Meriones, Eurypylus, Thoas and Odysseus. At Nestor’s word each marks a lot and throws it into Agamemnon’s helmet, and the army prays that the lot fall to Ajax, to Diomedes, or to Agamemnon himself.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then all became still in silence;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all fell hushed and silent;
sentences.n: Hector’s challenge is over and the army is stunned. ὣς ἔφαθ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes his speech at the end of the last part; ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο, elided, with the τ made θ before the rough breathing of οἱ. οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ‘and they then all’ are the Achaeans. ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ is a set phrase, found at 3.95 and in the Odyssey: ἀκήν ‘hushed’ and σιωπῇ ‘in silence’, with the same English each time.

sentences.t: αἴδεσθεν μὲν ἀνήνασθαι, δεῖσαν δ’ ὑποδέχθαι·
sentences.l: they were ashamed to refuse, but feared to take it up;
sentences.i: they were ashamed to refuse, yet afraid to take it up;
sentences.n: Why they are silent. αἴδεσθεν is the aorist of αἰδέομαι ‘feel shame’, in a third-plural form with the epic ending -εν, and δεῖσαν is the unaugmented aorist of δείδω ‘fear’. ἀνήνασθαι is the aorist infinitive of ἀναίνομαι ‘refuse’, and ὑποδέχθαι the aorist infinitive of ὑποδέχομαι ‘take up, accept’. The Greek names no object: what they refuse or take up is Hector’s challenge.

sentences.t:
ὀψὲ δὲ δὴ Μενέλαος ἀνίστατο καὶ μετέειπε
νείκει ὀνειδίζων, μέγα δὲ στεναχίζετο θυμῷ·
sentences.l:
Late at length Menelaus stood up and spoke among them,
reproaching with abuse, and he groaned greatly in his spirit:
sentences.i: At last, late, Menelaus rose and spoke among them, reproaching them with abuse, and he groaned deeply in his spirit:
sentences.n: Menelaus rises, late and angry. ὀψέ ‘late’ with δὴ ‘at length’ says that he stood up only after the long silence. ἀνίστατο ‘stood up’ is the imperfect middle of ἀνίστημι, and μετέειπε ‘spoke among them’ the epic aorist of μετεῖπον. νείκει is the dative of νεῖκος ‘strife, abuse’, ‘with abuse’, and goes with ὀνειδίζων ‘reproaching’ (as at 2.255). στεναχίζετο is ‘he groaned’, from στεναχίζω, with μέγα ‘greatly’ and θυμῷ ‘in his spirit’.

sentences.t: ὤ μοι ἀπειλητῆρες Ἀχαιΐδες οὐκέτ’ Ἀχαιοί·
sentences.l: “Oh me, threateners, Achaean women, no longer Achaeans;
sentences.i: “Oh me, you threateners, Achaean women and no longer Achaean men;
sentences.n: Menelaus’ speech opens with a cry of disgust. ὤ μοι ‘oh me’ is a cry of distress. ἀπειλητῆρες is the plural of ἀπειλητήρ ‘threatener’, from ἀπειλέω ‘threaten’: men who threaten and do no more. Ἀχαιΐδες οὐκέτ’ Ἀχαιοί ‘Achaean women, no longer Achaeans’ is the insult of 2.235; Ἀχαιΐδες is the feminine plural, so the army is called women.

sentences.t:
ἦ μὲν δὴ λώβη τάδε γ’ ἔσσεται αἰνόθεν αἰνῶς
εἰ μή τις Δαναῶν νῦν Ἕκτορος ἀντίος εἶσιν.
sentences.l:
Truly indeed this will be an outrage, dreadfully, terribly,
if no one of the Danaans now goes face to face with Hector.
sentences.i: This will be an outrage indeed, a dreadful, terrible one, if no man of the Danaans goes now to face Hector.
sentences.n: The disgrace he foresees. ἦ μὲν δή ‘truly indeed’ strengthens the claim, and λώβη is ‘outrage’ (as at 3.42). αἰνῶς is ‘terribly’; αἰνόθεν has the ending -θεν, which usually means ‘from’, but what it adds here is not known, so the pair is given as one doubled intensifier, ‘dreadfully, terribly’. εἰ μή τις … εἶσιν ‘if no one … goes’: εἶσιν is the third singular of εἶμι ‘go’, and after εἰ without ἄν the form can be read as an indicative or as an old subjunctive; the sense is the same. ἀντίος ‘face to face’ takes the genitive Ἕκτορος, and Δαναῶν is ‘of the Danaans’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὑμεῖς μὲν πάντες ὕδωρ καὶ γαῖα γένοισθε
ἥμενοι αὖθι ἕκαστοι ἀκήριοι ἀκλεὲς αὔτως·
sentences.l:
But you, all of you, may you become water and earth,
sitting right here, each one, spiritless, ingloriously, just so;
sentences.i: But as for you, may every one of you turn to water and earth, sitting right where you are, spiritless and without glory, for nothing;
sentences.n: A curse on his own side. γένοισθε ‘may you become’ is the aorist optative of wish, and ὕδωρ καὶ γαῖα ‘water and earth’ is what they are to become: the picture is of men who sit until they crumble away. ἥμενοι is the participle of ἧμαι ‘sit’, αὖθι ‘right here’, ἕκαστοι ‘each one’. ἀκήριοι is taken as ἀ- ‘not’ + κῆρ ‘heart’, ‘spiritless’; the Odyssey’s ἀκήριος at 12.98 is ‘uninjured’, so the sense here is chosen from the line, and the formation is not certain. ἀκλεές is a neuter used as an adverb, ‘without glory’, and αὔτως is ‘just so, to no purpose’.

sentences.t:
τῷδε δ’ ἐγὼν αὐτὸς θωρήξομαι· αὐτὰρ ὕπερθε
νίκης πείρατ’ ἔχονται ἐν ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσιν.
sentences.l:
but against this man I myself will arm; and above
the limits of victory are held among the immortal gods.”
sentences.i: but I myself will arm against him; and above us the limits of victory are held among the immortal gods.”
sentences.n: Menelaus will arm, and leaves the outcome to the gods. τῷδε ‘against this man’ (Hector) is a dative of opposition; ἐγών is ἐγώ with a movable ν; θωρήξομαι is the future middle of θωρήσσω ‘arm’. ὕπερθε ‘above’ opens the second clause and goes with ἔχονται. πείρατα are ‘limits’ (the word of πείρατα ὀλέθρου in the Odyssey, with the same English), here the limits of νίκη ‘victory’. ἔχονται is the middle-passive of ἔχω, ‘are held’, with ἐν ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσιν ‘among the immortal gods’. His speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας κατεδύσετο τεύχεα καλά.
sentences.l: So then, having spoken, he put on the fine armour.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and put on his fine armour.
sentences.n: The narrator takes over. ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ‘so then, having spoken’ is a stock opening. κατεδύσετο is an aorist of καταδύομαι ‘put on’ (literally ‘go down into’), in the sigma-aorist form -σετο for -σατο. τεύχεα καλά is ‘fine armour’, as at Odyssey 22.114.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά κέ τοι Μενέλαε φάνη βιότοιο τελευτὴ
Ἕκτορος ἐν παλάμῃσιν, ἐπεὶ πολὺ φέρτερος ἦεν,
sentences.l:
Then to you, Menelaus, would have appeared the end of life
in Hector’s hands, since he was much stronger,
sentences.i: Then, Menelaus, the end of your life would have shown itself at Hector’s hands, for he was far the stronger,
sentences.n: The poet speaks to Menelaus himself (Μενέλαε is a vocative) to say how near he came to dying. ἔνθά κέ τοι … φάνη ‘then to you would have appeared’: κε with the aorist indicative says what would have happened and did not, τοι is σοι ‘to you’, and φάνη is the aorist passive of φαίνω. The ‘if not’ that cancels it is in the next unit. βιότοιο τελευτή is ‘end of life’ (βίοτος ‘life’, as at 4.170), and Ἕκτορος ἐν παλάμῃσιν ‘in Hector’s hands’, παλάμη being ‘palm, hand’ with the dative plural -ῃσιν. φέρτερος is ‘stronger, better’, and ἦεν is ἦν.

sentences.t:
εἰ μὴ ἀναΐξαντες ἕλον βασιλῆες Ἀχαιῶν,
αὐτός τ’ Ἀτρεΐδης εὐρὺ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
δεξιτερῆς ἕλε χειρὸς ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν·
sentences.i: if the kings of the Achaeans had not sprung up and seized you; and Atreus’ son himself, wide-ruling Agamemnon, took you by the right hand and spoke, calling you by name:
sentences.n: The rescue. εἰ μὴ … ἕλον ‘if … had not seized’: the aorist indicative after εἰ μή is the past ‘if not’ that cancels the danger, ἀναΐξαντες is the aorist participle of ἀναΐσσω ‘spring up’, and ἕλον has no stated object (it is Menelaus). βασιλῆες Ἀχαιῶν is ‘kings of the Achaeans’. The sentence then slides from the ‘if not’ clause into plain narrative: ἕλε ‘took’ is told in the same indicative, with δεξιτερῆς … χειρός ‘by the right hand’ a genitive of the part grasped. Ἀτρεΐδης … Ἀγαμέμνων is ‘Atreus’ son, Agamemnon’, with εὐρὺ κρείων ‘wide-ruling’ printed as two words. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν is the stock line ‘spoke a word and called him by name’ (ἔκ … ὀνόμαζεν is a split verb), here with ‘you’ because the poet is still speaking to Menelaus.

sentences.t:
ἀφραίνεις Μενέλαε διοτρεφές, οὐδέ τί σε χρὴ
ταύτης ἀφροσύνης· ἀνὰ δὲ σχέο κηδόμενός περ,
sentences.l:
“You are acting senselessly, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, and not at all is there need for you
of this senselessness; but hold back, though you are distressed,
sentences.i: “You are acting senselessly, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, and you have no need at all of this senselessness. Hold yourself back, distressed though you are,
sentences.n: Agamemnon’s speech. ἀφραίνεις ‘you are acting senselessly’ is the verb of the participle at 2.258; διοτρεφές ‘Zeus-nurtured’ is the vocative of διοτρεφής, a stock address for kings. οὐδέ τί σε χρή ‘and not at all is there need for you’ takes the genitive ταύτης ἀφροσύνης ‘of this senselessness’. ἀνὰ … σχέο is a split verb, ἀνά + σχέο, the aorist imperative middle of ἀνέχω, ‘hold back, restrain yourself’; κηδόμενός περ is ‘though you are distressed’.

sentences.t:
μηδ’ ἔθελ’ ἐξ ἔριδος σεῦ ἀμείνονι φωτὶ μάχεσθαι
Ἕκτορι Πριαμίδῃ, τόν τε στυγέουσι καὶ ἄλλοι.
sentences.l:
and do not wish, out of strife, to fight with a man better than you,
Hector, Priam’s-son, whom others too hate.
sentences.i: and do not, out of rivalry, set yourself to fight a man better than you, Hector, son of Priam, whom others too hate.
sentences.n: What Agamemnon forbids. μηδ’ ἔθελ’ ‘and do not wish’ (μή + the imperative of ἐθέλω) takes the infinitive μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’ with the dative φωτὶ ἀμείνονι ‘a better man’; σεῦ is the epic genitive of σύ, ‘than you’. ἐξ ἔριδος ‘out of strife’ is out of rivalry. Πριαμίδῃ is the dative of the patronymic ‘son of Priam’, in apposition to Ἕκτορι. τόν τε στυγέουσι καὶ ἄλλοι ‘whom others too hate’: στυγέουσι is the uncontracted form of στυγοῦσι, and τε marks a general truth.

sentences.t:
καὶ δ’ Ἀχιλεὺς τούτῳ γε μάχῃ ἔνι κυδιανείρῃ
ἔρριγ’ ἀντιβολῆσαι, ὅ περ σέο πολλὸν ἀμείνων.
sentences.l:
And even Achilles, this man at least, in the man-glorifying battle
shudders to meet, he who is much better than you.
sentences.i: Even Achilles shudders to meet him in the battle that brings men glory, and he is far better than you.
sentences.n: Achilles is held up as the measure. καὶ δ’ is ‘and even’, and Ἀχιλεύς has a single λ for the metre. ἔρριγ’ is ἔρριγε, the perfect of ῥιγέω, with present sense ‘shudders’, and it takes the infinitive ἀντιβολῆσαι ‘to meet’ with the dative τούτῳ ‘him’. μάχῃ ἔνι κυδιανείρῃ is ἐν μάχῃ κυδιανείρῃ ‘in the man-glorifying battle’ (the epithet as at 4.225, with the same English), with ἔνι placed after its noun. ὅ περ ‘who indeed’ is Achilles, and σέο is the epic genitive of σύ after the comparative ἀμείνων ‘better’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν νῦν ἵζευ ἰὼν μετὰ ἔθνος ἑταίρων,
τούτῳ δὲ πρόμον ἄλλον ἀναστήσουσιν Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.l:
But you now sit down, going among the band of companions,
and for him another champion the Achaeans will raise up.
sentences.i: But you, go now and sit among the band of your companions, and the Achaeans will raise up another champion against him.
sentences.n: The advice: sit down, and the Achaeans will find another man. ἵζευ is the imperative of ἵζω ‘sit’, and ἰών ‘going’ with it makes ‘go and sit’. ἔθνος ἑταίρων is ‘the band of companions’: ἔθνος is a body of people who belong together, here his own circle. τούτῳ is the dative again, ‘against him’. πρόμον is ‘champion’ (as at 7.75), and ἀναστήσουσιν, the future of ἀνίστημι used with an object, is ‘will raise up’.

sentences.t:
εἴ περ ἀδειής τ’ ἐστὶ καὶ εἰ μόθου ἔστ’ ἀκόρητος,
φημί μιν ἀσπασίως γόνυ κάμψειν, αἴ κε φύγῃσι
δηΐου ἐκ πολέμοιο καὶ αἰνῆς δηϊοτῆτος.
sentences.l:
Even if he is fearless and is insatiate of the fray,
I say he will gladly bend the knee, if he escapes
from hostile war and fearsome fighting.”
sentences.i: Even if he is fearless and cannot have enough of the fray, I say he will bend his knee with joy, if he escapes from hostile war and fearsome fighting.”
sentences.n: The comfort. εἴ περ … καὶ εἰ ‘even if … and if’ gives two concessions: ἀδειής ‘fearless’ (ἀ- + δέος ‘fear’) and μόθου … ἀκόρητος ‘insatiate of the fray’, μόθος being the fray and ἀκόρητος ‘never full’ with the genitive. φημί μιν … κάμψειν ‘I say he will bend’: μιν is ‘him’, κάμψειν the future infinitive of κάμπτω. γόνυ κάμψειν ‘bend the knee’ is usually taken to mean he will be glad to rest, but the Greek says only ‘bend the knee’. ἀσπασίως is ‘gladly’. αἴ κε φύγῃσι is ‘if he escapes’: αἰ (= εἰ) + κε + the aorist subjunctive. The clause recurs at 173, and the last line is word for word 174. His speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν παρέπεισεν ἀδελφειοῦ φρένας ἥρως
αἴσιμα παρειπών, ὃ δ’ ἐπείθετο· τοῦ μὲν ἔπειτα
γηθόσυνοι θεράποντες ἀπ’ ὤμων τεύχε’ ἕλοντο·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the hero talked his brother’s mind round with what was fitting, and Menelaus obeyed; and then his attendants, glad, took the armour from his shoulders;
sentences.n: Menelaus gives way. ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ closes Agamemnon’s speech. παρέπεισεν is the aorist of παραπείθω ‘talk round, win over’, with ἀδελφειοῦ φρένας ‘his brother’s wits’ (ἀδελφειοῦ the genitive of ἀδελφειός, the epic form of ἀδελφός); ἥρως ‘the hero’ is Agamemnon, used as a title. αἴσιμα παρειπών is ‘having talked him round with things fitting’ (as at 6.62), and ὃ δ’ ἐπείθετο ‘and he obeyed’ is Menelaus, the imperfect middle of πείθω. τοῦ μέν is ‘of him’ (the article as a pronoun); γηθόσυνοι ‘glad’ and θεράποντες ‘attendants’ are the subject, and ἕλοντο is the middle aorist of αἱρέω, ‘took (off)’.

sentences.t: Νέστωρ δ’ Ἀργείοισιν ἀνίστατο καὶ μετέειπεν·
sentences.l: And Nestor among the Argives stood up and spoke among them:
sentences.i: And Nestor rose among the Argives and spoke:
sentences.n: Nestor rises. The Argives are the whole army (the poem’s three names for it are Achaeans, Danaans and Argives). ἀνίστατο καὶ μετέειπεν is the phrase used of Menelaus at 94 (there μετέειπε, without the final ν), with the same English in the word-for-word line; μετέειπεν ‘spoke among them’ is the aorist of μετεῖπον.

sentences.t: ὢ πόποι ἦ μέγα πένθος Ἀχαιΐδα γαῖαν ἱκάνει.
sentences.l: “Ah, truly a great grief comes to the Achaean country.
sentences.i: “Ah, truly a great grief is coming upon the Achaean country.
sentences.n: Nestor’s speech opens with a lament. ὢ πόποι is a cry, ‘ah’; ἦ is ‘truly’; πένθος is ‘grief’, and Ἀχαιΐδα γαῖαν is ‘the Achaean country’ (as at Odyssey 21.107), the accusative after ἱκάνει ‘comes to’. The grief he means is the army’s shame, which he spells out in the next lines.

sentences.t:
ἦ κε μέγ’ οἰμώξειε γέρων ἱππηλάτα Πηλεὺς
ἐσθλὸς Μυρμιδόνων βουληφόρος ἠδ’ ἀγορητής,
sentences.l:
Truly greatly would wail the old man, horse-driver Peleus,
good, of the Myrmidons counsel-bearer and speaker,
sentences.i: Peleus, the old horse-driver, would surely wail aloud, that good man, counsellor and speaker of the Myrmidons,
sentences.n: Nestor imagines how Peleus would take the news. ἦ κε … οἰμώξειε ‘truly would wail’ is a potential optative, with μέγα ‘greatly’. γέρων ἱππηλάτα Πηλεύς ‘the old man, horse-driver Peleus’ is built like the Odyssey’s γέρων ἱππηλάτα Νέστωρ and is translated the same way. Peleus is Achilles’ father, and the Myrmidons are Achilles’ people, though the Greek does not say so here. βουληφόρος ‘counsel-bearer’ and ἀγορητής ‘speaker’ are said of Peleus, and Μυρμιδόνων ‘of the Myrmidons’ depends on both.

sentences.t:
ὅς ποτέ μ’ εἰρόμενος μέγ’ ἐγήθεεν ᾧ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ
πάντων Ἀργείων ἐρέων γενεήν τε τόκον τε.
sentences.l:
who once, asking me, greatly rejoiced in his own house,
asking of all the Argives the lineage and the birth.
sentences.i: who once, in his own house, was greatly glad to question me, asking about the lineage and the birth of all the Argives.
sentences.n: Why Peleus would grieve. ὅς ‘who’ is Peleus. εἰρόμενος ‘asking’ is the participle of εἴρομαι with μ’ (με) ‘me’; ἐγήθεεν is the uncontracted imperfect of γηθέω ‘rejoice’, and ᾧ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ is ἐν ᾧ οἴκῳ ‘in his own house’ (ᾧ the possessive ὅς). ἐρέων is another participle ‘asking’, from ἐρέω, a form of the same verb; it takes the accusatives γενεήν τε τόκον τε ‘the lineage and the birth’, and πάντων Ἀργείων ‘of all the Argives’ depends on them, as the English line has it (the word-for-word line keeps the Greek order, so its ‘of all the Argives’ does not mean ‘asking them’). γενεήν ‘lineage’ and τόκον ‘birth’ together say who each man’s family was.

sentences.t:
τοὺς νῦν εἰ πτώσσοντας ὑφ’ Ἕκτορι πάντας ἀκούσαι,
πολλά κεν ἀθανάτοισι φίλας ἀνὰ χεῖρας ἀείραι
θυμὸν ἀπὸ μελέων δῦναι δόμον Ἄϊδος εἴσω.
sentences.l:
These now, if he heard that all were cowering beneath Hector,
many times he would lift up his dear hands to the immortals,
that his spirit from his limbs might sink into the house of Hades.
sentences.i: If he heard that they were all cowering before Hector, he would lift his dear hands to the immortals again and again, that his spirit might leave his limbs and go down into the house of Hades.
sentences.n: What would make Peleus pray for death. τοὺς … πάντας ‘all of them’ (the Argives) goes with πτώσσοντας ‘cowering’; ἀκούσαι is the aorist optative of ἀκούω, ‘if he heard’, an imagined case, and κε … ἀείραι ‘would lift up’ (the aorist optative of ἀείρω, with ἀνά split off) is what follows. πολλά is ‘much, again and again’. The Greek has no verb of praying: the raised hands are the prayer, and θυμὸν … δῦναι ‘that the spirit sink’ is the infinitive that says what he asks for, the spirit going ἀπὸ μελέων ‘from the limbs’ into δόμον Ἄϊδος εἴσω ‘the house of Hades’ (Ἄϊδος from Ἄϊς, a by-form of Ἅιδης).

sentences.t:
αἲ γὰρ Ζεῦ τε πάτερ καὶ Ἀθηναίη καὶ Ἄπολλον
ἡβῷμ’ ὡς ὅτ’ ἐπ’ ὠκυρόῳ Κελάδοντι μάχοντο
ἀγρόμενοι Πύλιοί τε καὶ Ἀρκάδες ἐγχεσίμωροι
Φειᾶς πὰρ τείχεσσιν Ἰαρδάνου ἀμφὶ ῥέεθρα.
sentences.l:
Would that — Father Zeus, and Athena, and Apollo —
I were young, as when by swift-flowing Celadon they fought,
gathered, the Pylians and Arcadians, spear-wielding,
by Pheia’s walls, around the streams of Iardanus.
sentences.i: If only — Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo — I were as young as when the Pylians and the spear-wielding Arcadians gathered and fought beside the swift-flowing Celadon, by the walls of Pheia, around the streams of the Iardanus.
sentences.n: Nestor wishes himself young again and begins a memory. αἲ γάρ ‘would that’ opens the wish, with the vocatives Ζεῦ πάτερ, Ἀθηναίη, Ἄπολλον; the first line is word for word 2.371, and its English is the same. ἡβῷμ’ is the optative of ἡβάω ‘be in youthful prime’, and ὡς ὅτε ‘as when’ begins the time he means. μάχοντο is the unaugmented imperfect ‘were fighting’, ἀγρόμενοι ‘gathered’ the aorist middle participle of ἀγείρω, and Πύλιοι and Ἀρκάδες ‘Pylians’ and ‘Arcadians’ are the two peoples. ἐγχεσίμωροι is ‘spear-wielding’ and ὠκυρόῳ ‘swift-flowing’. Κελάδοντι, Φειᾶς and Ἰαρδάνου are place names (a river Celadon, a town Pheia, the streams of the Iardanus); the Greek says no more about where they are.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ Ἐρευθαλίων πρόμος ἵστατο ἰσόθεος φὼς
τεύχε’ ἔχων ὤμοισιν Ἀρηϊθόοιο ἄνακτος
δίου Ἀρηϊθόου, τὸν ἐπίκλησιν κορυνήτην
ἄνδρες κίκλησκον καλλίζωνοί τε γυναῖκες·
sentences.l:
and against them Ereuthalion stood as champion, a man equal to a god,
having on his shoulders the armour of Areithous the lord,
heavenly Areithous, whom by surname club-wielder
men called, and fair-girdled women,
sentences.i: and against them Ereuthalion, a man the equal of a god, took his stand as champion, wearing on his shoulders the armour of lord Areithous, heavenly Areithous, whom men and fair-girdled women used to call the club-wielder, by surname,
sentences.n: The memory: the Arcadian champion. τοῖσι δ’ is ‘and against them’ (the Pylians and Arcadians), ἵστατο ‘took his stand’ the imperfect middle of ἵστημι, and πρόμος is ‘champion’. ἰσόθεος φώς ‘a man equal to a god’ is the stock phrase, with the same English every time. Ereuthalion is the man Nestor says at 4.319 that he killed. He wears the armour of Ἀρηϊθόοιο ἄνακτος ‘Areithous the lord’, the club-wielder of 7.8–10, with δίου Ἀρηϊθόου ‘heavenly Areithous’ in apposition. τὸν ἐπίκλησιν κορυνήτην … κίκλησκον is ‘whom they used to call, by surname, the club-wielder’: ἐπίκλησιν is an accusative ‘by way of surname’, κίκλησκον the imperfect of κικλήσκω, the reduplicated present of καλέω (the -σκ- belongs to the present stem and is not the iterative suffix), and καλλίζωνοι ‘fair-girdled’ (as in the Odyssey).

sentences.t:
οὕνεκ’ ἄρ’ οὐ τόξοισι μαχέσκετο δουρί τε μακρῷ,
ἀλλὰ σιδηρείῃ κορύνῃ ῥήγνυσκε φάλαγγας.
sentences.l:
because he did not fight with bows nor with a long spear,
but with an iron club he used to break the battle-lines.
sentences.i: because he did not fight with bows or a long spear, but used to break the battle-lines with an iron club.
sentences.n: Why he was called club-wielder. οὕνεκ’ ἄρ’ is ‘because, you see’. μαχέσκετο and ῥήγνυσκε are iterative imperfects (the -σκ- marks what he did again and again), ‘used to fight’ and ‘used to break’. τόξοισι δουρί τε μακρῷ is ‘with bows or a long spear’ after οὐ, σιδηρείῃ κορύνῃ ‘with an iron club’, and φάλαγγας ‘battle-lines’.

sentences.t:
τὸν Λυκόοργος ἔπεφνε δόλῳ, οὔ τι κράτεΐ γε,
στεινωπῷ ἐν ὁδῷ ὅθ’ ἄρ’ οὐ κορύνη οἱ ὄλεθρον
χραῖσμε σιδηρείη· πρὶν γὰρ Λυκόοργος ὑποφθὰς
δουρὶ μέσον περόνησεν, ὃ δ’ ὕπτιος οὔδει ἐρείσθη·
sentences.l:
Him Lycurgus killed by a trick, not at all by strength,
in a narrow road, where then not the club for him destruction
warded off, the iron one; for before that Lycurgus, forestalling him,
with a spear pierced him through the middle, and he on his back was driven to the ground;
sentences.i: Lycurgus killed him by a trick, not at all by strength, in a narrow road, where the iron club did not ward off destruction for him; for Lycurgus got in first and pierced him through the middle with a spear, and he was driven down on his back onto the ground;
sentences.n: How Areithous died. τόν is ‘him’ (Areithous), ἔπεφνε the aorist of φένω ‘killed’, δόλῳ ‘by a trick’, and κράτεΐ the dative of κράτος ‘strength’. Λυκόοργος is spelled ‘Lycurgus’ as at 6.130; the Greek does not say whether it is the same man. ὅθ’ is ὅθι ‘where’, elided: the θ shows it, since ὅτε ‘when’ would stand as ὅτ’ before the smooth breathing of ἄρ’. χραῖσμε is the aorist of χραισμέω ‘ward off’, with ὄλεθρον ‘destruction’ and the dative οἱ ‘for him’. ὑποφθάς is the aorist participle of ὑποφθάνω ‘get in first, forestall’. περόνησεν is ‘pierced’, μέσον ‘through the middle’, ὕπτιος ‘on his back’, and ἐρείσθη the aorist passive of ἐρείδω ‘press, drive’.

sentences.t: τεύχεα δ’ ἐξενάριξε, τά οἱ πόρε χάλκεος Ἄρης.
sentences.l: and the armour he stripped off, which to him gave bronze Ares.
sentences.i: and he stripped off the armour that Ares in bronze had given him.
sentences.n: The spoils. ἐξενάριξε is the aorist of ἐξεναρίζω ‘strip of armour’; the verb can mean kill and strip, but only the stripping is told here, with τεύχεα ‘armour’ as its object. τά οἱ πόρε is ‘which gave him’, with οἱ the dative ‘to him’ and πόρε the unaugmented aorist of πορεῖν ‘give’. χάλκεος Ἄρης ‘Ares in bronze’ is the war-god himself, said to have given the arms to Areithous.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὰ μὲν αὐτὸς ἔπειτα φόρει μετὰ μῶλον Ἄρηος·
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ Λυκόοργος ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἐγήρα,
δῶκε δ’ Ἐρευθαλίωνι φίλῳ θεράποντι φορῆναι·
τοῦ ὅ γε τεύχε’ ἔχων προκαλίζετο πάντας ἀρίστους.
sentences.i: He himself then wore these arms into the toil of battle; but when Lycurgus grew old in his halls, he gave them to his dear attendant Ereuthalion to wear, and wearing that armour Ereuthalion kept challenging all the best men.
sentences.n: How the armour came to Ereuthalion. καὶ τὰ μέν ‘and these’ is answered by αὐτάρ ‘but’ in line 148. φόρει is the imperfect of φορέω ‘wear’, and μετὰ μῶλον Ἄρηος ‘into the toil of Ares’ has Ἄρης standing for battle, as at 2.401. ἐγήρα is ‘grew old’ (from γηράω), ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ‘in his halls’, and φορῆναι is the epic infinitive of φορέω, ‘to wear’. θεράπων is ‘attendant’, and φίλῳ ‘dear’. τοῦ ‘his’ is Lycurgus’; προκαλίζετο ‘kept challenging’ is as at 4.389, and πάντας ἀρίστους ‘all the best’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ μάλ’ ἐτρόμεον καὶ ἐδείδισαν, οὐδέ τις ἔτλη·
ἀλλ’ ἐμὲ θυμὸς ἀνῆκε πολυτλήμων πολεμίζειν
θάρσεϊ ᾧ· γενεῇ δὲ νεώτατος ἔσκον ἁπάντων·
sentences.i: But they trembled greatly and were afraid, and no one could bring himself to face him; but my much-enduring spirit urged me on to fight, in its own boldness; and I was the youngest of them all in age;
sentences.n: Nobody answers the challenge but Nestor. οἳ δέ ‘and they’ are the men challenged; ἐτρόμεον ‘were trembling’ is the imperfect of τρομέω, ἐδείδισαν ‘were afraid’ a past form of δείδω, and οὐδέ τις ἔτλη is ‘and no one brought himself’ (τλάω, as in the Odyssey), the thing he could not bring himself to do being left unsaid. ἀλλ’ ἐμέ … ἀνῆκε is ‘but me … urged on’ (the aorist of ἀνίημι, as in Apollo’s question at 7.25), with θυμὸς πολυτλήμων ‘a much-enduring spirit’ and πολεμίζειν ‘to fight’. θάρσεϊ ᾧ is ‘in its own boldness’, ᾧ being the possessive ὅς, agreeing with θάρσεϊ and looking back to the spirit. γενεῇ is ‘in birth’, that is in age, and ἔσκον is an old iterative form of εἰμί, ‘I was’.

sentences.t: καὶ μαχόμην οἱ ἐγώ, δῶκεν δέ μοι εὖχος Ἀθήνη.
sentences.l: And I was fighting with him, and Athena gave me the boast.
sentences.i: And I fought him, and Athena gave me the triumph.
sentences.n: Nestor takes up the fight and wins. μαχόμην οἱ ἐγώ is ‘I was fighting with him’, μαχόμην the imperfect and οἱ the dative ‘with him’. δῶκεν … εὖχος ‘gave … the boast’ is as at 5.285 and 7.81, with the same English: εὖχος is what one can boast of, ‘triumph’ in the English line. Athena is named as the giver.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὴ μήκιστον καὶ κάρτιστον κτάνον ἄνδρα·
πολλὸς γάρ τις ἔκειτο παρήορος ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα.
sentences.l:
That man, the tallest and strongest, I killed;
for a huge man lay there stretched out here and there.
sentences.i: I killed that man, the tallest and the strongest; for he lay there huge, stretched out this way and that.
sentences.n: The size of the man he killed. τὸν δή ‘that very one’ is taken up by ἄνδρα at the end of the line, ‘that man … the man’. μήκιστον ‘tallest’ and κάρτιστον ‘strongest’ are superlatives (μήκιστοι is ‘the tallest’ in the Odyssey, κάρτιστοι ‘the strongest’ at 1.266), and κτάνον is the unaugmented aorist ‘killed’. πολλὸς … τις is ‘a huge man’, ἔκειτο ‘lay’, and ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα ‘here and there’. The sense of παρήορος here is not known: it is built on παρά ‘beside’ and the root of ἀείρω ‘lift’, and elsewhere describes a horse harnessed beside the others, so ‘stretched out’ is a guess taken from the line.

sentences.t:
εἴθ’ ὣς ἡβώοιμι, βίη δέ μοι ἔμπεδος εἴη·
τώ κε τάχ’ ἀντήσειε μάχης κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ.
sentences.l:
If only I were so young, and my strength were firm;
then soon would meet battle Hector of the glancing helmet.
sentences.i: If only I were as young as that, and my strength were firm; then Hector of the glancing helmet would soon have a fight to face.
sentences.n: The wish for youth returns. εἴθ’ is ‘if only’, ὣς ‘so’, ἡβώοιμι the optative of ἡβάω, and ἔμπεδος ‘firm’. τώ is ‘then, in that case’. ἀντήσειε is the aorist optative of ἀντάω ‘meet’, which takes the genitive, so μάχης is ‘meet battle’, that is ‘have a fight to face’. κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ is ‘Hector of the glancing helmet’, his stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
ὑμέων δ’ οἵ περ ἔασιν ἀριστῆες Παναχαιῶν
οὐδ’ οἳ προφρονέως μέμαθ’ Ἕκτορος ἀντίον ἐλθεῖν.
sentences.l:
And of you, those who are the best of the Achaeans all together,
not even they are readily eager to go against Hector.”
sentences.i: And even those of you who are the best of all the Achaeans are not readily eager to go against Hector.”
sentences.n: Nestor’s reproach reaches the leaders. ὑμέων is the epic genitive plural of σύ, ‘of you’. οἵ περ ἔασιν ἀριστῆες Παναχαιῶν is ‘those who really are the best of the Achaeans all together’ (ἔασιν is εἰσίν; Παναχαιῶν as at 2.404). οὐδ’ οἳ ‘not even those’ takes the same men up again. μέμαθ’ is μέματε, the second plural of the perfect of μέμονα ‘be eager’, elided, with the τ made θ before the rough breathing of Ἕκτορος: the person is ‘you’, matching the ὑμέων that opened the sentence, with οἳ ‘who’ as subject, so ‘they’ in the word-for-word line and ‘those of you’ in the English line are the same men. And προφρονέως is ‘readily’ (as at 5.810). ἀντίον ἐλθεῖν is ‘to go against’. His speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς νείκεσσ’ ὃ γέρων, οἳ δ’ ἐννέα πάντες ἀνέσταν.
sentences.l: So the old man reviled, and they, nine in all, stood up.
sentences.i: So the old man reviled them, and all nine stood up.
sentences.n: The effect of Nestor’s reproach. νείκεσσ’ is the elided, unaugmented aorist of νεικέω, ‘reviled’ (as at 6.325), with ὁ γέρων ‘the old man’. οἳ δ’ ἐννέα πάντες is ‘and they, nine in all’, and ἀνέσταν is the epic aorist of ἀνίστημι in its intransitive sense, = ἀνέστησαν, ‘stood up’. The nine are named in the next lines: Agamemnon, Diomedes, the two Ajaxes, Idomeneus, Meriones, Eurypylus, Thoas and Odysseus.

sentences.t:
ὦρτο πολὺ πρῶτος μὲν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων,
τῷ δ’ ἐπὶ Τυδεΐδης ὦρτο κρατερὸς Διομήδης,
sentences.l:
Rose by far the first the lord of men, Agamemnon,
and after him rose the son of Tydeus, strong Diomedes,
sentences.i: By far the first to rise was the lord of men, Agamemnon, and after him rose the son of Tydeus, strong Diomedes,
sentences.n: The nine rise in order. ὦρτο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι in its intransitive sense, ‘rose’. πολὺ πρῶτος is ‘by far first’, and ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων ‘Agamemnon, lord of men’. τῷ δ’ ἐπί is ‘and after him’; Τυδεΐδης ‘the son of Tydeus’ is Diomedes, and κρατερός ‘strong’.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἐπ’ Αἴαντες θοῦριν ἐπιειμένοι ἀλκήν,
τοῖσι δ’ ἐπ’ Ἰδομενεὺς καὶ ὀπάων Ἰδομενῆος
Μηριόνης ἀτάλαντος Ἐνυαλίῳ ἀνδρειφόντῃ,
sentences.l:
and after them the two Ajaxes, clothed in impetuous might,
and after them Idomeneus and Idomeneus’ follower,
Meriones, the equal of Enyalius, killer of men,
sentences.i: and after them the two Ajaxes, clothed in impetuous might, and after them Idomeneus and Idomeneus’ follower Meriones, the equal of Enyalius, killer of men,
sentences.n: Four more rise. τοῖσι δ’ ἐπ’ is ‘and after them’. Αἴαντες is the plural for the two men named Ajax. θοῦριν ἐπιειμένοι ἀλκήν is ‘clothed in impetuous might’: θοῦρις is the feminine adjective ‘impetuous’, and ἐπιειμένοι the perfect middle participle of ἐπιέννυμι ‘clothe’, the same as at Odyssey 9.214. ὀπάων Ἰδομενῆος is ‘Idomeneus’ follower’, a man who attends and follows a leader; he is named in the next line as Μηριόνης ‘Meriones’. ἀτάλαντος Ἐνυαλίῳ ἀνδρειφόντῃ is ‘the equal of Enyalius, killer of men’, Ἐνυάλιος being a name of Ares. Line 166 is metrically irregular as transmitted: its fifth foot is a spondee, and Ἐνυαλίῳ has to be scanned with synizesis, the -ιῳ as one syllable.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἐπ’ Εὐρύπυλος Εὐαίμονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός,
ἂν δὲ Θόας Ἀνδραιμονίδης καὶ δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l:
and after them Eurypylus, Euaemon’s splendid son,
and up rose Thoas, Andraemon’s-son, and heavenly Odysseus;
sentences.i: and after them Eurypylus, Euaemon’s splendid son; and up rose Thoas, son of Andraemon, and heavenly Odysseus;
sentences.n: The last three. Εὐρύπυλος Εὐαίμονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός is ‘Eurypylus, Euaemon’s splendid son’ (as at 2.736). ἂν δέ is ἀνά ‘up’ + δέ, with ὦρτο ‘rose’ understood from the line before. Ἀνδραιμονίδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Andraemon’, and δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς ‘heavenly Odysseus’. Line 167 is metrically irregular as transmitted: in the third foot the short final syllable of Εὐρύπυλος has to be taken as long before the vowel of Εὐαίμονος.

sentences.t: πάντες ἄρ’ οἵ γ’ ἔθελον πολεμίζειν Ἕκτορι δίῳ.
sentences.l: All these then were willing to fight with heavenly Hector.
sentences.i: All of them were willing to fight heavenly Hector.
sentences.n: The nine are ready. πάντες ἄρ’ οἵ γ’ is ‘all these then’, ἔθελον the imperfect of ἐθέλω ‘were willing’, and πολεμίζειν Ἕκτορι δίῳ ‘to fight heavenly Hector’, with the dative Ἕκτορι after the verb.

sentences.t: τοῖς δ’ αὖτις μετέειπε Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.l: And among them again spoke the Gerenian horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: The Gerenian horseman Nestor spoke among them again:
sentences.n: Nestor speaks again. τοῖς δ’ αὖτις μετέειπε is ‘and among them again spoke’, αὖτις ‘again’ because he spoke last at 123. Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ is his stock name, translated every time; the meaning of Γερήνιος is disputed (Gerenia, a place in Messenia, or a link with γέρων ‘old man’ or γέρας ‘honour’), and no choice is made. ἱππότα is the old nominative of ἱππότης ‘horseman’.

sentences.t: κλήρῳ νῦν πεπάλασθε διαμπερὲς ὅς κε λάχῃσιν·
sentences.l: “By lot now cast, right through, whoever gets it;
sentences.i: “Now cast lots right through, for whoever is allotted it;
sentences.n: Nestor proposes lots. κλήρῳ is ‘by lot’ (dative); πεπάλασθε is the reduplicated aorist imperative middle of πάλλω ‘shake’, so ‘cast lots’. διαμπερές is ‘right through’; the Greek does not say through what, and the English leaves it as it is. ὅς κε λάχῃσιν is ‘whoever gets it’: λάχῃσιν is the aorist subjunctive of λαγχάνω ‘obtain by lot’, and κε makes it ‘whoever it may be’.

sentences.t:
οὗτος γὰρ δὴ ὀνήσει ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς,
καὶ δ’ αὐτὸς ὃν θυμὸν ὀνήσεται αἴ κε φύγῃσι
δηΐου ἐκ πολέμοιο καὶ αἰνῆς δηϊοτῆτος.
sentences.i: for this man will indeed do good to the well-greaved Achaeans, and he will do good to his own spirit too, if he escapes from hostile war and fearsome fighting.”
sentences.n: Why the lot matters. οὗτος γὰρ δή is ‘for this man indeed’; ὀνήσει is the future of ὀνίνημι ‘benefit, profit’, and ὀνήσεται its middle future, so that he profits his own θυμός ‘spirit’, here his life, and ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς is ‘the well-greaved Achaeans’. καὶ δ’ αὐτός is ‘and he himself too’. Line 174 is word for word 119, with the same English, and αἴ κε φύγῃσι ends 173 as it ended 118. His speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δὲ κλῆρον ἐσημήναντο ἕκαστος,
ἐν δ’ ἔβαλον κυνέῃ Ἀγαμέμνονος Ἀτρεΐδαο.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they marked a lot, each one,
and cast in the helmet of Agamemnon, Atreus’-son.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and each of them marked a lot and threw it into the helmet of Agamemnon, son of Atreus.
sentences.n: The lots. ὣς ἔφαθ’ closes Nestor’s speech. οἳ δέ ‘and they’ are the nine; ἐσημήναντο is the aorist middle of σημαίνω ‘mark (for oneself)’, with κλῆρον ‘a lot’ and ἕκαστος ‘each one’ in the singular after a plural verb; the Greek does not say how the lots were marked. ἐν δ’ ἔβαλον is ‘and they threw in’, κυνέῃ the dative of κυνέη ‘helmet’, and Ἀγαμέμνονος Ἀτρεΐδαο ‘of Agamemnon, Atreus’ son’ with the epic genitive -αο.

sentences.t:
λαοὶ δ’ ἠρήσαντο, θεοῖσι δὲ χεῖρας ἀνέσχον·
ὧδε δέ τις εἴπεσκεν ἰδὼν εἰς οὐρανὸν εὐρύν·
sentences.l:
And the people prayed, and to the gods lifted their hands,
and thus kept saying someone, looking to the wide heaven:
sentences.i: The troops prayed and held up their hands to the gods, and thus would some man say, looking up to the wide heaven:
sentences.n: The army prays. λαοί are ‘the people, the troops’, ἠρήσαντο the aorist of ἀράομαι ‘pray’, and θεοῖσι δὲ χεῖρας ἀνέσχον ‘and lifted their hands to the gods’. The first line is word for word 3.318, with the same English; 3.319 went on to name Achaeans and Trojans, but here the second line is new. ὧδε δέ τις εἴπεσκεν is ‘and thus someone kept saying’, εἴπεσκεν an iterative of εἶπον, ‘would say’. ἰδών ‘looking’ is the aorist participle of ὁράω, and εἰς οὐρανὸν εὐρύν ‘to the wide heaven’ is as at 3.364.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ ἢ Αἴαντα λαχεῖν, ἢ Τυδέος υἱόν,
ἢ αὐτὸν βασιλῆα πολυχρύσοιο Μυκήνης.
sentences.l:
“Father Zeus, either Ajax to obtain the lot, or the son of Tydeus,
or the king himself of Mycenae rich in gold.”
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, let Ajax draw the lot, or the son of Tydeus, or the king himself of Mycenae rich in gold.”
sentences.n: The prayer itself. The Greek has no main verb: Ζεῦ πάτερ calls on the god, and ἢ … ἢ … ἢ ‘either … or … or’ lists three men with the infinitive λαχεῖν (the aorist of λαγχάνω ‘obtain by lot’), so the wish is ‘[grant] that Ajax get it, or Tydeus’ son, or the king’; the English supplies ‘let’. Αἴαντα is one Ajax, in the singular, and Τυδέος υἱόν ‘the son of Tydeus’ is Diomedes. αὐτὸν βασιλῆα … Μυκήνης is ‘the king himself of Mycenae’, Agamemnon, with πολυχρύσοιο ‘rich in gold’ (as in the Odyssey). The speech ends here.
